analysis.title: Asia in Focus - China: Property Downturn Deeper Than Previously Anticipated, But Its Growth Drag Should Still Ease Gradually in the Years Ahead
key_insights: China's property downturn is in its sixth year. Most housing activity indicators have been weaker than GS expected so far in 2026.
The recent policy shift from presales to completed-home sales implies tighter developer funding and lower property investment over the next few years.
GS estimates the property sector's share of China's real GDP at around 15% currently, versus nearly 30% at its peak. It expects the share to fall to around 8% from 2030 onward.

GS estimates the direct drag on real GDP growth from property at 1.8pp in 2026, slightly above 1.7pp in 2025 and above its previous 2026 estimate of 1.5pp. It expects the drag to narrow by around 0.5pp to 1.3pp in 2027 and largely fade by 2030.
The direct drag sums five channels: construction, real estate services, upstream effects through commodity demand, move-in related consumption and land-sales related fiscal effects.
In January-September 2026, land sales revenue fell 28% yoy, new home starts fell 25% yoy and property FAI fell 21% yoy, all weaker than GS expected at the start of the year.
Most activity indicators, including new home starts, sales and property FAI, are down 60-90% from their 2020-21 peaks.

GS's property research team lowered forecasts for new home starts, completions, sales and property FAI in the 2027 outlook. From 2025 to 2035 they expect starts to drop another 30%, completions 46%, property FAI 61% and new home sales 70%.
GS's new baseline has land sales revenue, new home starts, new home sales and property FAI declining another 20%, 20%, 10% and 17% in 2027, after drops of 30%, 22%, 8% and 20% expected in 2026.
Property construction is deeper and more protracted than previously anticipated because the government aims to significantly reduce new home supply.

Home prices in top-tier cities such as Shanghai and Shenzhen, where inventory is already low, may begin to recover soon. Prices in lower-tier cities with large inventory overhangs may keep falling for several years.

GS's property research team projects a more than 90% decline in residential land sales volume from 2025 to 2035. This implies persistent local government financing pressure and the need for alternative revenue or spending cuts.

GS sees scope for a nationwide property tax expansion toward the end of the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30) or during the 16th (2031-35). Timing depends on housing market conditions and domestic confidence.

The indirect housing wealth effect amplifies the growth impact and peaked in 2024-25. GS expects it to fade by the early 2030s, assuming existing home prices bottom in 2030. It does not change the conclusion that the drag diminishes gradually.

Model changes: floor space under construction is re-estimated from new home starts because stuck projects distort NBS data, and Ministry of Finance land sales revenue replaces the discontinued NBS land-purchase series.

risk_factors: Tighter developer funding and lower property investment from the shift to completed-home sales.
Persistent local government financing pressure from the projected 90%+ fall in residential land sales volume, especially in regions most dependent on property revenue.
Continued price declines in lower-tier cities with large inventory overhangs.
Negative household housing wealth effect, since property is around half of household assets.
